author: maya-chen
title: Why Your Body Doesn't Believe You're Safe
dek: Your mind knows nothing is wrong, yet your chest stays tight. Here is what the vagus nerve has to do with it.
seo_title: Nervous System Regulation: When Your Body Doesn't Feel Safe
seo_description: Your mind knows nothing is wrong, yet your chest stays tight. A plain look at nervous system regulation and what the vagus nerve has to do with it.
pull_quote: Changing what your body is doing changes the data your brain receives.
body_html:
It's late on an ordinary weeknight. Nothing is wrong, and you know it. And yet your jaw is clenched, your chest feels tight, and your mind keeps replaying a conversation from last week.

If you have ever asked yourself, Why can't I just relax?, I want you to hear this: you are not failing to relax. Your nervous system is doing exactly what it was built to do.

The part of you that lives below thought

Most anxiety advice is aimed at the thinking brain, the part of you that can reason and recognize that a threat isn't real. That work matters. But the system running the alarm sits deeper, in structures like the brainstem, and it doesn't speak in thoughts. It speaks in sensation. That is why you can know you're safe and still feel like your body is bracing for impact.

A main line between that system and your organs is the vagus nerve. Its name comes from the Latin for "wandering," and it earns it: it runs from the base of your skull through your throat, heart and lungs, all the way into your gut. When it is working well, your body gets a steady, quiet signal: safe, calm, connected.

The traffic runs mostly upward

By the classic anatomical counts, done in animals, roughly 80% of the fibers in the vagus nerve carry signals from the body up to the brain, not the other way around (Foley & DuBois, 1937; Prescott & Liberles, 2022). Your gut, heart and lungs are constantly reporting in, and your brain is listening.

So when your breath is quick and shallow, your brain can read that as evidence of danger. Telling yourself "I'm fine" is working against the current. Changing what your body is doing changes the data your brain receives.

Changing what your body is doing changes the data your brain receives.

In 1994, Stephen Porges introduced polyvagal theory, a model of three states your nervous system moves through: ventral vagal (safe and social), sympathetic (fight or flight) and dorsal vagal (shutdown). Researchers still debate parts of the theory, but the map can be a useful one. Many anxious people describe cycling between the last two, wired at midnight and collapsed by noon, with only brief visits to the first.

Your body learned this for a reason

Think of a smoke detector installed too close to the stove. It goes off when you make toast. It isn't broken. It is calibrated for a level of danger that made sense somewhere else.

Bessel van der Kolk has long argued, in a 1994 paper and later in The Body Keeps the Score (2014), that trauma can be stored in the body as somatic memory, not only as a story you can recall. You never decided to stay on alert. Your body decided for you, and that decision kept you going. The problem isn't that it made the wrong call. Nobody ever told it the emergency was over.

A small practice for tonight. Sit with your feet on the floor. Notice your jaw, then your shoulders, then your belly. Ask yourself which state you're closest to right now, and simply name it, with no judgment. Then let one slow exhale out through slightly parted lips, longer than your inhale, and feel your shoulders drop even a little.

These practices are meant to support professional care, not replace it. If you take medication for anxiety, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

If this resonated, my book Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety walks through these ideas step by step.
source: Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety, Chapters 1 and 2
banner: Your mind knows. Your [body] is still [catching up].

author: maya-chen
title: The Longer Exhale: A Bedtime Practice for Anxiety
dek: A gentle four-minute wind-down that uses a longer exhale and a little humming to tell your nervous system the day is done.
seo_title: Breathing Exercises for Sleep: The Longer Exhale at Bedtime
seo_description: A gentle four-minute wind-down: a breathing exercise for sleep that pairs a longer exhale with soft humming to tell your body the day is done.
pull_quote: The key is that the exhale is longer than the inhale.
body_html:
You're exhausted, but you can't turn off. Your body wants to collapse and your mind keeps reviewing the day: the call you handled badly, the pile of work waiting for tomorrow.

That gap between tired and rested isn't a character flaw. It's a timing problem. Your nervous system doesn't know the day is over. It is still waiting for an "all clear" signal it never received. An evening practice is a way to send that signal on purpose.

Why the exhale matters

Your heart rate naturally rises a little as you breathe in and slows a little each time you breathe out, a rhythm the vagus nerve helps set. When you make the exhale longer than the inhale, you lean into that slowing. Slow breathing makes that rhythm bigger, and longer exhales may too (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014), though studies disagree on whether a longer exhale adds much beyond the slower pace itself (Meehan & Shaffer, 2024).

You don't need to hit a perfect number. The key is that the exhale is longer than the inhale.

The key is that the exhale is longer than the inhale.

The evening wind-down, step by step

A safety note first: if counting your breath ever triggers anxiety or makes you feel disconnected, use the humming step on its own for the first week. Humming alone is a complete evening practice.

Sit on the edge of your bed or on a bathroom stool. The whole sequence takes about four minutes.

  1. Settle. Feel your feet on the floor. Take one breath without managing it, and notice its quality: is it shallow, held or rapid?
  2. Extend the exhale. Inhale through your nose for 4 slow counts. Exhale through your nose or slightly parted lips for 8 slow counts. If 8 feels strained, try 6. Continue for about 2 minutes (roughly 8 to 10 cycles). Keep your jaw soft and let your hands rest open on your thighs.
  3. Transition. Get up and brush your teeth, continuing to breathe slowly if you can.
  4. Hum. With your mouth closed, hum on a comfortable low note: a song, a single tone or a simple "hmmmm." Feel the vibration in your chest and throat. Continue for 2 minutes while you brush, walk to bed and settle the covers.
  5. Close. Lying down, take three slow extended exhales. Set your phone face down or outside the room. Notice the weight of your body against the mattress. Rest.

What you might notice

Your thoughts may slow during the humming, or your limbs may feel heavy. Both can be signs of your body settling toward rest. Restlessness or an urge to check your phone often eases if you stay with the humming. Sometimes unexpected sadness or warmth surfaces as you settle, and that is completely normal.

If lying flat is uncomfortable, the breathing works well propped on pillows or in a recliner. If you feel self-conscious humming near a partner, keep it barely audible. Even at low volume, a hum still stretches out your exhale.

If you take medication for anxiety or sleep, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

Try it tonight. Before you pick up your toothbrush, give yourself three breaths of 4 counts in and 8 counts out. Then notice what your body does.

The full morning and evening routine lives in Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety, if you'd like to go further.
source: Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety, Chapter 4 (Exercise 4B, The Evening Wind-Down Sequence)
banner: Breathe out [longer] than you breathe in.

author: maya-chen
title: Nervous System Regulation for Beginners: A 3-Minute Start
dek: New to nervous system regulation? Learn what it means, the three states polyvagal theory describes, and a gentle 3-minute check-in to try today.
seo_title: Nervous System Regulation for Beginners: A 3-Minute Start
seo_description: New to nervous system regulation? Learn what it means, the three states polyvagal theory describes, and a gentle 3-minute check-in to try today.
pull_quote: None of these states is your fault. All of them are information.
body_html:
It's the middle of an ordinary day. Nothing is wrong, your inbox is under control, and your shoulders are still up near your ears. You sit down to rest and your body doesn't come with you. Somewhere you read that you need nervous system regulation, and you nodded, and you have no idea what to do with that.

Let's start there, because the phrase gets used far more often than it gets explained. If you're a beginner, you only need two things today: a rough map of the states your body moves through, and one small way of checking where you are.

What nervous system regulation means

Nervous system regulation is a loose, everyday phrase for how your body moves into a stress response and finds its way back out. It doesn't mean feeling calm all day, and it doesn't mean you stop getting activated. It means you stop staying there.

And if you've been stuck for a long time, please hear this: your nervous system isn't broken. It's been protecting you with the tools it had. The work now is giving it better ones.

Three states, as polyvagal theory maps them

The most familiar map comes from polyvagal theory, which Stephen Porges first set out in a 1994 presidential address, published in 1995. It describes three circuits in the autonomic nervous system, each tied to a different state (Porges, 2022). In everyday terms, they might feel like this:

Ventral vagal is safety and connection. Your breathing is easy, conversation feels natural, and problems feel solvable.

Sympathetic is fight or flight. Your heart works harder than the situation requires, your thoughts speed up, and your jaw, shoulders and belly brace without asking you first.

Dorsal vagal is shutdown. The world goes grey, flat and far away. You feel heavy and slow.

These are positions, not personality types.

In the theory, the sympathetic and dorsal responses are ways of surviving threat, so nobody is asking you to get rid of them. None of these states is your fault. All of them are information. The goal is more time in ventral, and an easier road back to it.

None of these states is your fault. All of them are information.

I want to be honest about the map, too. Polyvagal theory is a theory, and scientists still debate it. In a 2023 paper, the researcher Paul Grossman argued that each of its basic premises is "either untenable or highly implausible." Porges, for his part, has kept refining the theory and responding to its critics (Porges, 2025). So hold the three states as words for noticing your body, not as settled anatomy.

Why regulation starts in the body

Your vagus nerve is one of the main lines between your organs and your brain, and much of its traffic runs upward. It is the principal relay for sensory information from your lungs, and its sensory fibers are the main sensory supply to your heart (Prescott & Liberles, 2022).

So how you're breathing and how your heart is beating are part of what your brain is working with. If someone has ever told you to calm down and nothing happened, you already know that telling doesn't reach everything. Thinking work is valuable and it has its place. The body is simply another way in.

It's hard to change what you can't notice, which makes a check-in a kind place for a beginner to start.

The Nervous System Check-In, step by step

This is a practice from my book, a way of paying attention. It isn't a tested clinical protocol.

A safety note first: if you carry a trauma history or tend to feel floaty or disconnected when you turn your attention inward, go slowly. Keep your eyes open if closed eyes feel unsafe, and pause to look around the room any time it feels like too much.

Find a comfortable seat with your feet flat on the floor, or lie down if that's easier. The whole practice takes about 2 to 3 minutes. Give each of the first six steps about 10 seconds.

  1. Settle. Place both hands in your lap, palms up. Take one normal breath and notice it without changing it.
  2. Jaw. Is it clenched or easy? Notice whether your teeth are touching. No fixing yet.
  3. Shoulders. Are they lifted toward your ears?
  4. Belly. Is it soft or braced? Does your breath reach your lower abdomen, or does it stop at your chest?
  5. Heart area. Is there tightness, heaviness, openness or warmth? Put a word or a color to it, whatever arrives first.
  6. Name it. Which state are you closest to right now: ventral, sympathetic or dorsal? Just name it, with no judgment.
  7. Exhale. Take one slow breath out through slightly parted lips, longer than your inhale. Feel your shoulders drop even a millimeter. Return to the room.

What you might notice

You might be surprised by how much tension you're carrying. That isn't something to fix right now. You might struggle to locate any sensation at all, and that's allowed too. A small wave of emotion can surface as well.

If sitting upright is uncomfortable, try this on your back with your knees bent and your feet flat on the floor. If you feel overwhelmed or very floaty, open your eyes, look around the room and name five things you can see before you continue.

What regulation can feel like

It doesn't have to feel like bliss. It might be a small release of breath, your shoulders dropping half an inch, a moment of quiet between thoughts. Deb Dana calls these glimmers, "micro-moments of regulation that foster feelings of well-being," and part of this practice is learning to catch them before they pass unnoticed.

The first run doesn't make you a runner, but the first run still counts.

If you'd like a simple way to begin, try checking in three times today: morning, midday and evening. And this week, when a difficult email arrives and your chest tightens before you've finished reading, bring your attention to your exhale. One extended breath out, as slow as you can make it. Notice what your nervous system does.

These practices are meant to support professional care, not replace it. If you take medication for anxiety, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

If you want to understand more of the why, read why your body doesn't believe you're safe. For something to do with your breath, try two breathing exercises for when you're stressed. And if you'd like to see what my book Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety is like before anything else, you can peek inside at a full practice from it.
source: Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety, Chapters 1, 2 and 3 (Exercise 01, The Nervous System Check-In)

author: maya-chen
title: Breathing Exercises to Calm Down When You're Stressed
dek: Two breathing exercises to calm down when stress spikes: a sigh for under a minute, a slow exhale for three, and what the research really shows.
seo_title: Breathing Exercises to Calm Down When You're Stressed
seo_description: Two breathing exercises to calm down when stress spikes: a sigh for under a minute, a slow exhale for three, and what the research really shows.
body_html:
It's 11:47 in the morning and you're about to walk into a meeting you've been dreading. Your jaw is clenched, your shoulders are somewhere near your ears, and your heart has already decided this is an emergency. You don't have ten minutes for a breathing session. You have ninety seconds in a bathroom stall.

Someone has probably told you to take a deep breath. It's kind advice and it doesn't tell you much. How long? In through what? These two breathing exercises to calm down come with the actual steps: one for when you have under a minute, one for when you have three.

Being stressed in your body doesn't mean you're handling your life badly.

What a breathing exercise can and can't do

Slow, deliberate breathing can help some people feel less stressed. In a 2023 meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials, Fincham and colleagues linked breathwork with lower self-reported stress than control conditions, and the effect held in the ten trials of slow-paced breathing. The effect was small to medium, and the authors asked readers to interpret it cautiously.

The results weren't significant for groups living with mental or physical health conditions, though their numbers were close to the others, and the authors say that may reflect how few people were studied.

Think of these two practices as circuit breakers, not renovations.

Circuit breakers, not renovations.

Why your breath is worth working with

Your heart speeds up slightly as you inhale and slows slightly as you exhale. The name for that rhythm is respiratory sinus arrhythmia, and your vagus nerve is part of it (Lehrer & Gevirtz, 2014).

A longer exhale is often sold as the whole secret. The research is less tidy. In a small 2014 experiment with 30 people, Van Diest and colleagues found that breathing out for more than twice as long as breathing in led people to report more relaxation than the reverse pattern. In 2024, Meehan and Shaffer measured heart rate variability at six breaths a minute and found a 1:2 ratio did no better than even breaths, and the earlier studies they reviewed disagreed with each other. They measured different things, so nobody has the last word.

Take the long exhale as an invitation and not a formula. If it steadies you, keep it. If even breaths feel better, that counts.

Before you begin

A safety note: if you have asthma or COPD, check with your physician before practicing extended exhale breathing. If you're prone to lightheadedness or hyperventilation, go slowly and shorten the exhale at first. If you feel dizzy, return to normal breathing right away. And if you carry trauma or tend to dissociate, breathwork can occasionally feel activating rather than settling. You can stop and breathe naturally at any point.

Practice one: the physiological sigh

This is the one for the bathroom stall. It's a double inhale through the nose followed by a long, slow exhale. Sighing isn't foreign to your body, either: sighs happen on their own every few minutes to re-inflate the tiny air sacs in your lungs (Li et al., 2016).

Here's what the study actually did. In a 2023 randomized trial from Stanford (Balban et al., Cell Reports Medicine), 108 people, mostly undergraduates, spent five minutes a day for a month on one of four practices: cyclic sighing, box breathing, cyclic hyperventilation or mindfulness meditation. All four groups felt less anxious after their daily session. Cyclic sighing brought a bigger lift in positive mood than mindfulness, and a bigger drop in breathing rate. On anxiety, breathwork and mindfulness came out about even, and heart rate variability didn't differ between the groups. The authors describe the study as exploratory, and it was too small to rank the breathing styles against each other.

The version below is much shorter than what they tested, so think of it as a quick taste of the practice.

Find a seated or standing position. This takes 30 to 60 seconds.

  1. Inhale fully through your nose for 4 counts.
  2. Without exhaling, take a second, shorter sniff on top of the first, as if you're topping off a nearly full glass.
  3. Exhale slowly and completely through your mouth, lips slightly parted, for 6 to 8 counts. Let your shoulders drop on the way out.
  4. Pause naturally at the bottom of the exhale for 1 to 2 seconds.
  5. Return to normal breathing and notice the quality of your next few breaths.

You can repeat up to 3 cycles. If the double inhale feels uncomfortable, try a single full inhale followed by the long exhale. If you need to be quiet, exhale through your nose; people in the Stanford trial could breathe entirely through the nose.

Practice two: the longer exhale

This is the one for when you have a few minutes.

Find a comfortable seated position. This takes 1 to 3 minutes.

  1. Place one hand on your belly and let it rest there, without pressing.
  2. Inhale through your nose for 4 counts. Feel your belly rise before your chest.
  3. Without pausing, exhale slowly through slightly parted lips for 6 counts.
  4. If that feels comfortable after a few cycles, extend the exhale to 8 counts. Leave the inhale at 4.
  5. Continue for 6 to 10 breath cycles and let the rhythm become automatic.
  6. Return to your natural breath and notice how things feel now.

If counting feels like too much when you're stressed, whisper a long "shhhh" on the exhale instead.

What you might notice

Your shoulders or jaw may feel heavier. You might yawn or sigh without meaning to, or feel a little drowsy. Feeling nothing is also normal, and a quiet first try doesn't tell you much: in the Stanford trial, the lift in mood from sighing grew the more days people kept at it. If the count feels forced, drop to 4 in and 5 out and build from there.

This week, when a difficult call ends and you're still holding the phone, bring your attention to your shoulders. Try one physiological sigh before you do anything else. Then notice what your nervous system does.

These practices are meant to support professional care, not replace it. If your symptoms are new or keep coming back, a doctor can check that a physical problem isn't behind them. If you take medication for anxiety, please talk with your doctor before changing anything.

If the evenings are your hardest time, the longer exhale at bedtime adapts this same breath for winding down. If you're not sure where to begin, start with nervous system regulation for beginners. And if you'd like to see what my book Vagus Nerve Exercises for Anxiety is like, you can peek inside at a full practice from it.
